title: Mercury and the Woodman
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Woodman was felling a tree on the bank of a river, when his axe, glancing off the trunk, flew out of his hands and fell into the water. As he stood by the water's edge lamenting his loss, Mercury appeared and asked him the reason for his grief; and on learning what had happened, out of pity for his distress he dived into the river and, bringing up a golden axe, asked him if that was the one he had lost.

The Woodman replied that it was not, and Mercury then dived a second time, and, bringing up a silver axe, asked if that was his. "No, that is not mine either," said the Woodman. Once more Mercury dived into the river, and brought up the missing axe. The Woodman was overjoyed at recovering his property, and thanked his benefactor warmly; and the latter was so pleased with his honesty that he made him a present of the other two axes.

When the Woodman told the story to his companions, one of these was filled with envy of his good fortune and determined to try his luck for himself. So he went and began to fell a tree at the edge of the river, and presently contrived to let his axe drop into the water. Mercury appeared as before, and, on learning that his axe had fallen in, he dived and brought up a golden axe, as he had done on the previous occasion. Without waiting to be asked whether it was his or not the fellow cried, "That's mine, that's mine," and stretched out his hand eagerly for the prize: but Mercury was so disgusted at his dishonesty that he not only declined to give him the golden axe, but also refused to recover for him the one he had let fall into the stream.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Woodman lose his axe?
options: It slips from his grip while he is resting
It is stolen by a passing traveller
It glances off the trunk and flies into the water
It breaks in half while he is chopping

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury first bring up from the river?
options: A golden axe
A silver axe
The Woodman's own axe
A bronze axe

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Woodman say about the golden axe?
options: That it was exactly the one he had lost
That he did not want any axe at all
That he wanted to keep it regardless
That it was not the one he had lost

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury do once the Woodman is honest about both axes?
options: He gives him only his own axe back
He gives him all three axes as a present
He asks the Woodman to work for him
He takes all three axes away with him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the envious companion do to try his luck?
options: He borrows the Woodman's axe to use himself
He waits by the river for Mercury to appear
He lets his own axe drop into the water on purpose
He asks the Woodman to introduce him to Mercury

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the companion cry out when Mercury brings up the golden axe?
options: "That's mine, that's mine"
"Is that truly mine?"
"I am not sure that is mine"
"Please, keep it for yourself"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury refuse to do for the dishonest companion?
options: Speak to him again for the rest of his life
Allow him to fell any more trees by the river
Tell him where the golden axe came from
Give him the golden axe or recover his own lost axe

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Mercury reward the first Woodman with all three axes?
options: He wants the Woodman to have a spare axe for emergencies
He is pleased by the Woodman's honesty in refusing axes that were not his
He feels sorry that the Woodman works so hard for so little
He is testing whether the Woodman can carry all three at once

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the companion's plan fail so completely?
options: Mercury does not appear for him at all
He drops his axe in the wrong part of the river
His eagerness to claim an axe that wasn't his reveals his dishonesty
He forgets to ask Mercury for help in time

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Telling the truth, even against your own interest, is rewarded in the end
Rivers are dangerous places to work with sharp tools
Mercury only helps those who ask him directly for gold
Working with a friend is safer than working alone

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the Woodman doing when he loses his axe?
options: Building a small boat by the water
Chopping wood already lying on the ground
Repairing a fence near the riverbank
Felling a tree on the bank of a river

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury bring up on his second dive?
options: A golden axe
A silver axe
The Woodman's own axe
An empty net

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who does the Woodman tell about his good fortune?
options: The local king
A group of strangers
His companions
No one at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the companion deliberately drop his axe in the river?
options: He hopes to repeat the first Woodman's good fortune
He wants to test whether Mercury actually exists
He is trying to retrieve something else from the river
He accidentally drops it while imitating the Woodman's work

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the companion's instant claim on the golden axe reveal about him?
options: He recognizes the axe immediately as his own
He is more honest than the first Woodman
He does not understand what Mercury is offering him
He is willing to claim something that he knows is not truly his

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Woodman was "lamenting" his loss?
options: Celebrating an unexpected gain
Expressing sorrow over it
Ignoring it completely
Explaining it calmly to a friend

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Two Woodmen share the same three axes equally
Mercury refuses to help either Woodman who loses an axe
An honest Woodman is rewarded, while a dishonest imitator loses even what he had
A Woodman tricks Mercury into giving him extra axes
